research_concepts: Within-game play-type sequence (teammate DRIVE preceding PNR)
Carryover effect from prior possession’s play type on PNR efficiency
methodological_questions: How accurately are DRIVE possessions identified, given documented foul leakage and low confidence?
How reliable is the temporal link from a DRIVE possession to the immediately following PNR possession for the same team?
Can confounding by defensive adjustments, game situation, and lineup be controlled with the available data?
Will the number of clean DRIVE-then-PNR sequences be sufficient for adequate power?
Does leakage of foul-ending possessions into OTHER and misclassification of DRIVE undermine PPP measures on both legs?

historical_evidence.finding: Play-type label accuracy/distribution audit failed: OTHER 20.2% vs <10% target; 40.8% low confidence; DRIVE foul-draw 1.7% vs 14-22% benchmark; most play types’ PPP above benchmark band; MIA identity checks fail. Verdict: tool_eval_fail.

Play-type label backfill verification failed: PNR share 28.7% (fail, band 20-28%); PULL_UP 7.9% fail; 3,100 games with team PNR >33% fail; team identity fail; 82.8% of PNR labels proxy_calibrated. Final verdict: FAIL.

OTHER/DRIVE foul leakage artifact found: OTHER 36% foul endings inflate PPP; DRIVE 12 percentage points below foul benchmark; only 0.7% of possessions map to a real play type via initiation_type. Verdict: artifact_found.
A1 adaptation falsification tests indicate effects are artifacts of labeling flaws, with wrong-way, neutral, and no-signal groups not showing the expected gradient, and no carryover to next game.

On-ball defensive scheme labels (DROP/ICE/SWITCH) could be assigned to only 14.9% (DET) and 3.3% (ORL) of half-court possessions, and switches_on was unpopulated; scheme classifications are too sparse for use as controls.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Systematic audit of play-type label quality (volume, foul rates, PPP, identity) against benchmarks
failed_approaches.why: DRIVE foul-draw rate far below acceptable range (1.7% vs 14-22%); 40.8% low-confidence; MIA identity checks fail. Labels contain systematic errors that make fine-grained comparisons unreliable.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Verification of backfilled play-type labels against league distributions and team-specific checks
failed_approaches.why: PNR share too high (28.7%), many team PNR shares exceed plausible bounds, 82.8% of PNR labels required proxy calibration, and team identity tests failed.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Attempt to use play-type PPP as a measure of offensive efficiency
failed_approaches.why: Foul-ending possessions leak into the OTHER category, inflating its PPP, while DRIVE is severely depleted of fouls, making PPP comparisons across play types artifacts of the labeling pipeline.

evidence_establishes: The derived play-type labels (including DRIVE and PNR) suffer from high rates of misclassification, low confidence, and systematic foul leakage (FAM:SF-APPM-014, FAM:SF-APPA-030, FAM:SF-CHT-025).

DRIVE possessions in particular have a foul-draw rate far below any realistic benchmark (1.7% vs 14-22%), indicating that many actual DRIVE possessions are either mislabeled or missing foul elements (FAM:SF-APPM-014).
PNR labels are over-expanded and calibrated via proxy, raising questions about whether each PNR label corresponds to a true pick-and-roll possession (FAM:SF-APPA-030).
Attempts to draw causal inferences from play-type sequences (e.g., adaptation/carryover) have produced artifacts when labels are used (FAM:SF-APPA-001).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a real causal effect of a teammate’s DRIVE on subsequent PNR efficiency exists.
The true proportion of possessions that are correctly labeled as both DRIVE and PNR in sequence.
That defensive scheme information can be measured well enough to control for confounding (FAM:SF-APPS-058).
That any observed PPP difference would reflect offensive carryover rather than label noise or selection effects.
own_inferences: Because DRIVE and PNR labels both have substantial error, the joint probability of correctly identifying a DRIVE-then-PNR sequence is extremely low, likely causing severe attenuation bias and spurious findings.
The expected sample of clean DRIVE-then-PNR sequences would be too small to achieve adequate statistical power even if a subset of labels could be salvaged.
Unmeasured confounders (defensive adjustments triggered by the DRIVE, lineup changes, game state) are likely correlated with both the occurrence of a DRIVE and the subsequent PNR’s success.
Any positive or negative association would be indistinguishable from artifacts of the labeling pipeline.
uncertainties: Whether the labeling pipeline will be improved in the future to enable reliable sequence-based analyses.
Whether a manual annotation of a small sample could reveal a true effect, though that would not constitute an answer based on the available database.
The exact magnitude of the bias introduced by foul leakage into OTHER and depletion from DRIVE on PPP calculations for this specific sequence.

historical_effect.explanation: Without the historical records, a researcher might proceed to test the hypothesis using the derived play-type labels. The retrieved families—especially the diagnosis of severe DRIVE label failures (FAM:SF-APPM-014, FAM:SF-CHT-025), PNR label overcalibration (FAM:SF-APPA-030), and the artifact outcomes in adaptation tests (FAM:SF-APPA-001)—show conclusively that the labeling infrastructure cannot support the required exposure and outcome measurement. This changed the decision from a potentially proceedable question to a clear do_not_proceed.

blocking_constraints.text: DRIVE label has severe foul-draw miscalibration (1.7% vs 14-22% benchmark) and low confidence; PNR label is over-expanded and proxy-calibrated. A DRIVE-then-PNR sequence requires both labels to be correct, which is very rare.
Foul-ending possessions leak into OTHER and are depleted from DRIVE, distorting PPP for both the preceding DRIVE and the target PNR if foul possessions intervene or are misassigned.

The number of cleanly labeled DRIVE-then-PNR sequences is likely too small to detect realistic effect sizes, given that only ~60% of possessions are labeled with adequate confidence and DRIVE misclassification further reduces the pool.

Defensive scheme adjustments, game situation, remaining shot-clock, and lineup changes following a DRIVE are likely to affect the subsequent PNR’s efficiency, and defensive scheme labels are too sparse to control for them (FAM:SF-APPS-058).
Selecting on the occurrence of a prior DRIVE may condition on a noisy label, inducing regression-to-the-mean effects in both the exposure and the outcome PPP.

prior_work.summary: Multiple prior audits have found that the play-type labeling system produces unreliable DRIVE and PNR labels due to systematic miscalibration, foul leakage, and low confidence. Adaptation/carryover studies using these labels have already been flagged as artifactual. While no prior study directly tested the DRIVE-before-PNR PPP hypothesis, the infrastructure necessary to test it has been shown to be unfit for purpose.

risks.text: DRIVE possession identification is fundamentally broken (foul-draw rate 1.7% vs benchmark 14-22%); many DRIVE possessions are likely not recorded as such, and vice versa.
Foul possessions misattributed to OTHER/DRIVE distort PPP and can cause lookahead bias if the possession outcome influences the label.
Cleanly labeled sequences will be rare; even with multi-season data, cell sizes may be too small for reliable inference.
Defensive adjustments, game clock, and lineup are uncontrolled and correlated with both the decision to DRIVE and subsequent PNR outcomes.
Conditioning on a DRIVE labeled by a noisy process may introduce selection bias and regression to the mean.
If multiple sequence-combinations are explored, the risk of false positives increases without pre-registration, though this is secondary to the labeling issues.

design.estimand: Average difference in points per possession (PPP) on PNR possessions that immediately follow a teammate’s DRIVE possession, compared to PNR possessions that follow a non-DRIVE half-court possession, among the same team and within the same game segment, conditional on correct play-type labels.
design.unit: Possession (the PNR possession as outcome unit; the preceding possession defines the exposure of interest).
design.sample: All half-court possessions from the 2022-23 through 2025-26 seasons where a team runs a PNR, with the immediately prior offensive possession by the same team classified as DRIVE or non-DRIVE. Exclude transition, end-of-quarter, and possessions with missing or low-confidence labels.
design.power: With estimated ~2-3% of PNR possessions having a correctly labeled prior DRIVE, the expected sample of a few hundred exposed possessions would provide ~0.20 power to detect a 0.10 PPP difference at α=0.05 (two-sided). This is grossly inadequate.
design.controls: Game state (period, margin, possession start time remaining), offensive lineup (starter/bench composition), defensive scheme if available (but scheme labels are too sparse), opponent defensive rating, home/away.
design.falsification: Repeat the analysis using randomly permuted preceding-play-type labels; a real effect should disappear under permutation. Test whether PPP on DRIVE possessions themselves predicts PNR success (a direct causal link would be implausible). Check whether the effect holds when restricting to high-confidence labels only.
design.multiplicity: Pre-register the single primary contrast (prior DRIVE vs non-DRIVE). Report all other explored contrasts as secondary with Bonferroni correction.
design.decision_rule: Interpret only if the overall audit of used labels passes pre-specified gate criteria (e.g., DRIVE foul-draw rate within 10-25%, PNR share within 18-26%, label confidence ≥ 0.7). Given current data, this gate cannot be met.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 play-by-play and derived play-type possession records as of 2026-06-14. Per-game files from NBA stats API with play-by-play, rotations, starters, matchups, box-score summaries, and Neo4j play-type possession graph.

methodological_questions: confounding by game state or defensive adjustment
sample size and sparsity of drive-then-PNR sequences
potential for lookahead bias in labeling
args.query: Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR points per possession

reasoning_details.text: We are in Stage 1. We need to identify research concepts and methodological questions, then call retrieve_history. The research question: "Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP." Concepts: DRIVE (play type), PNR (pick and roll), PPP (points per possession), teammate drive preceding a PNR, play-type labeling, data quality. Methodological questions: How to link plays? How to define "preceding"? How to measure PPP? How to handle multiple drives? Selection bias? What data is available? Let's identify concepts: "teammate drive", "PNR", "PPP", "play sequence", "play-type labeling". Methodological questions: "temporal linking of plays", "confounding factors", "sample size", "measurement of PPP for PNR after a drive", "definition of 'preceding'". Query: "drive before pick and roll points per possession". Let's construct the retrieve_history call.

We are in Stage 2. We have the retrieval results. We need to complete steps 4-9 and output the JSON. But first, we can use follow-up tools if needed (within 12 total, we've used 1 so far). The retrieval gave many families, some relevant. We should read key families to get full details, especially those directly about play-type labeling and DRIVE/PNR. Let's identify which are most relevant.

The research question: "Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP." This is about sequences: a DRIVE play type then a PNR play type, and whether the PNR's points per possession is higher when preceded by a DRIVE (by any teammate) versus not. This involves temporal linking of consecutive possessions with correct labeling of DRIVE and PNR. The data includes play-by-play with derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points). So we need to know if DRIVE and PNR labels are reliable, if possessions can be linked sequentially, if we can identify "teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR", and if any confounders exist.

Relevant families returned:
- FAM:SF-APPM-058: PNR shot-level season rates vs possession labels. Not directly about DRIVE or sequences, but about PNR labeling. Not a hypothesis test. Might show PNR rates.
- FAM:SF-APPM-014: Play-type label accuracy / distribution audit. Very relevant: it found systematic issues with play type labels, including DRIVE foul-draw low, OTHER high, etc. Overall FAIL. This raises LABEL_ERROR, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER risks.
- FAM:SF-APPS-036: Player-level BEST vs AVOID PPP gap (initiators). Not directly relevant.
- FAM:SF-APPA-030: Play-type label backfill verification. Also label quality issues: PNR 28.7% FAIL, PULL_UP FAIL, team identity FAIL. Final FAIL. Label error risk.

This shows significant labeling flaws for DRIVE and PNR (PNR foul rate 22%). The finding "DRIVE: 12pp below foul benchmark (FOUL_LEAK)" means DRIVE possessions are missing fouls, which leak into OTHER. This could affect PPP of DRIVE and PNR if we need to link them. However, the question is about PNR PPP given a preceding DRIVE; the reliability of DRIVE label and foul assignment matters.
- FAM:SF-APPA-001: A1 adaptation falsification. Not directly relevant, but shows label error and mechanical floor risks.
- FAM:SF-APPA-005: Defensive scheme change. Label error risk, but not about DRIVE/PNR sequences.
- FAM:SF-APPA-056: TRANSITION gradient subgroup. Not relevant.

So the main historical evidence concerns serious play-type label quality issues, particularly for DRIVE and PNR. This could make the question untestable or likely artifact. We need to assess testability.

We should read the full records of FAM:SF-APPM-014, FAM:SF-CHT-025, FAM:SF-APPA-030 to get detailed findings, failure mechanisms, sample sizes. Also FAM:SF-APPM-058 maybe for PNR label context. Also check if any study addressed sequential possession linking. The retrieval didn't return any study on sequential analysis of DRIVE then PNR. Then maybe explore_graph on some nodes for risks and limitations. But careful with budget: we have 11 remaining calls. We'll use read_family calls, then maybe glossary or data_catalog for definitions of play types and possession linking. Also we can check if "DRIVE" and "PNR" are defined in the data catalog.

Let's start with read_family for 014, 025, 030. That's 3 calls. Then we can examine data_catalog and glossary to understand the data fields and definitions. We'll reserve budget for explore_graph if needed.

But we also have SF-APPA-030 already in results with a summary. The question involves a DRIVE preceding a PNR. The core is about sequence of play types: any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP. That is a causal question about carryover from one possession to the next within a game. Key issues: play type labeling accuracy, especially for DRIVE and PNR; the temporal linking; sample size of such sequences; confounding by defense adjustment, game state, etc.

Retrieval returned many families showing severe labeling problems: FAM:SF-APPM-014 (FAIL audit), FAM:SF-APPA-030 (backfill verification FAIL), FAM:SF-CHT-025 (OTHER/DRIVE foul leakage artifact), and FAM:SF-APPA-001 (artifact from labeling). Also defensive scheme labeling issues (SF-APPS-058) and adaptation tests that failed. This suggests that any analysis relying on play type labels, especially DRIVE and PNR, is severely compromised.

We need to produce the final response following the schema. First, we need to list historical evidence from the returned records. I'll extract relevant records that directly speak to labeling and sequence. Then failed approaches: e.g., play type label audits that failed, showing systematic issues. Evidence establishes that current play type labels (including DRIVE and PNR) have substantial inaccuracies, leakage, and low confidence. Does not establish that DRIVE-then-PNR sequence PPP is testable. Own inferences: the question is likely untestable with current data due to label errors. Uncertainties include whether after fixing labeling, there might be a real effect, but current state is insufficient. Testability p_testable low. Decision: do_not_proceed, or proceed_with_changes if labeling is fixed? But we're asked to decide before any analysis is run with this data. Given multiple audits showing label failures, we should likely recommend do_not_proceed.

We need to cite the specific records returned. I'll use FAM:SF-APPM-014, FAM:SF-APPA-030, FAM:SF-CHT-025, FAM:SF-APPA-001. Also other records like FAM:SF-APPS-058 on defensive scheme labels, but that's less direct. The question involves DRIVE and PNR PPP. The PPP measure itself might be affected by foul leakage, as shown in FAM:SF-CHT-025. Also the DRIVE label has low foul draw rate (1.7% vs 14-22% benchmark), so DRIVE possessions are likely mislabeled or missing fouls, which would affect DRIVE identification. If we cannot reliably identify DRIVE possessions, we cannot test the sequence.

Thus, the design would require reliable play type labels. But the data catalog may reveal additional fields. Let's explore data catalog to confirm what per-game files contain. But we might not need to, as the question hinges on labeling. But we can check if there are alternative ways to define "DRIVE" from PBP action types without relying on the derived play-type labels. The question statement says "Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP." The DRIVE and PNR are presumably from "derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play." So we rely on those labels. The audits indicate those labels are unreliable. So testability is low.

I'll structure the final response accordingly. Let's first summarize historical evidence from the records:

- FAM:SF-APPM-014 (status: not a hypothesis test): Play-type label accuracy/distribution audit FAIL. Result: OTHER 20.2% vs <10% target; 40.8% low confidence; DRIVE foul-draw 1.7% vs 14-22% benchmark; most PTs PPP above benchmark band; MIA identity checks fail. Verdict: tool_eval_fail.
- FAM:SF-APPA-030 (status: inconclusive): Play-type label backfill verification FAIL. PNR share 28.7% FAIL; PULL_UP 7.9% FAIL; 3100 games with team PNR >33% FAIL; team identity FAIL. Final: FAIL.
- FAM:SF-CHT-025 (status: artifact): Play-type labeling audit: OTHER/DRIVE foul leakage. Found OTHER PPP inflated by 36% foul endings; DRIVE 12pp below foul benchmark; only 0.7% map to a real play type via initiation_type. Verdict: artifact_found.
- FAM:SF-APPA-001 (status: artifact): A1 adaptation falsification tests show artifact due to labeling issues.

Failed approaches: the play-type labeling pipeline as a whole has systematic errors, foul leakage, and volume mis-calibration, making it unsuitable for fine-grained studies like DRIVE-then-PNR sequences.

What evidence establishes: The derived play-type labels (including DRIVE and PNR) suffer from high uncertainty, miscalibration, and leakage of foul possessions, undermining any analysis that depends on accurate identification of DRIVE possessions and their connection to subsequent PNR efficiency.

Evidence does not establish: That a DRIVE preceding a PNR actually influences PNR efficiency; the question remains unanswered but untestable with current data quality.

Own inferences: The sparsity of clean DRIVE-then-PNR sequences (given label confidence only ~60% and DRIVE misclassification) would likely result in severely underpowered analysis even if labeling could be partially corrected. Additionally, confounding from defensive adjustments (e.g., if a DRIVE led to a defensive reaction that changes PNR coverage) would require reliable defensive scheme measures, which are also problematic (SF-APPS-058). Therefore, the question as posed cannot be reliably tested.
